rows.stem: If A is a square matrix of order 2 and \(\left|\mathrm{A}\right| = -2\), then value of \(\left|5\mathrm{A}'\right|\) is :
rows.solution: Transposing a matrix leaves its determinant unchanged, so \(\left|\mathrm{A}'\right| = \left|\mathrm{A}\right| = -2\). For a square matrix of order \(n\), \(\left|k\mathrm{A}\right| = k^{n}\left|\mathrm{A}\right|\), because each of the \(n\) rows contributes one factor of \(k\). Here \(n = 2\) and \(k = 5\), so \(\left|5\mathrm{A}'\right| = 5^{2}\left|\mathrm{A}'\right| = 25 \times (-2) = -50\), which is option (A) \(-50\). Treating \(k\) as a single factor gives \(5 \times (-2) = -10\), which is exactly why \(-10\) is offered as a distractor.

rows.stem: The product of matrix P and Q is equal to a diagonal matrix. If the order of matrix Q is \(3 \times 2\), then order of matrix P is :
rows.solution: The product \(\mathrm{PQ}\) exists only when the number of columns of P equals the number of rows of Q, which is 3. So P has order \(m \times 3\) for some \(m\), and then \(\mathrm{PQ}\) has order \(m \times 2\). A diagonal matrix is by definition square, so \(m \times 2\) forces \(m = 2\). Hence P is of order \(2 \times 3\), which is option (C) \(2 \times 3\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.solution: The sine function takes the value 1 only at \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi\), so \(\sin(xy) = 1\) forces the product \(xy\) to be one of those constants. Differentiating \(xy = \text{constant}\) with respect to \(x\) gives \(y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\), that is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{y}{x}\), which is option (D) \(-\dfrac{y}{x}\). Differentiating the relation exactly as printed instead gives \(\cos(xy)\left(y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0\), which says nothing here, since \(\cos(xy) = 0\) at every point where \(\sin(xy) = 1\); it is the constancy of \(xy\) that settles the derivative.

Substitute \(t = \cot\theta\), so that \(dt = -\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\theta\, d\theta\) and the limits become \(t = \cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\) and \(t = \cot\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\cot\theta\;\mathrm{cosec}^{2}\theta\;d\theta = \int_{1}^{0} t\,(-dt) = \int_{0}^{1} t\,dt = \left[\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Equivalently the antiderivative is \(-\dfrac{\cot^{2}\theta}{2}\), and \(0 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\); losing the minus sign carried by \(dt\) is what produces the distractor \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Take the 4 out of the radical: \(\sqrt{9 - 4x^{2}} = 2\sqrt{\dfrac{9}{4} - x^{2}}\). Hence \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{9 - 4x^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2} - x^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3/2}\right) + c = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{3}\right) + c\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{3}\right) + c\). Differentiating that back confirms the constant: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2/3}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{4x^{2}}{9}}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{9 - 4x^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9 - 4x^{2}}}\).

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: The area of the region bounded by the curve \(y^2 = 4x\) and \(x = 1\) is :
rows.solution: The parabola \(y^{2} = 4x\) is symmetric about the X-axis, and the line \(x = 1\) meets it at \((1, 2)\) and \((1, -2)\). Taking twice the part above the axis, the required area is \(2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} y\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{1} 2\sqrt{x}\,dx = 4\left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{8}{3}\) square units, which is option (B) \(\dfrac{8}{3}\). Integrating only the upper half and forgetting to double it gives \(\dfrac{4}{3}\), the first distractor.

rows.stem:
The general solution of the differential equation

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x + y}\) is :
rows.solution: Since \(e^{x+y} = e^{x}e^{y}\), the variables separate: \(\dfrac{dy}{e^{y}} = e^{x}\,dx\), i.e. \(e^{-y}\,dy = e^{x}\,dx\). Integrating both sides gives \(-e^{-y} = e^{x} + k\), and rearranging, \(e^{x} + e^{-y} = c\) where \(c = -k\) is an arbitrary constant. That is option (A) \(e^{x} + e^{-y} = c\).

rows.stem:
If a \(= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) and

b \(= \tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{3}\right) - \cot^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\)

then find the value of a + b.
rows.solution: Read every inverse function on its principal branch. Since \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), we have \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\); and because \(\cos^{-1}\) takes its values in \([0, \pi]\), \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Hence \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{3\pi + 8\pi}{12} = \dfrac{11\pi}{12}\). Next, \(\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), and since \(\cot^{-1}\) takes its values in \((0, \pi)\), a negative argument gives an obtuse angle: \(\cot^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \pi - \cot^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). So \(b = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Therefore \(a + b = \dfrac{11\pi}{12} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{11\pi - 4\pi}{12} = \dfrac{7\pi}{12}\).

rows.stem: Sand is pouring from a pipe at the rate of 15 cm\(^3\)/minute. The falling sand forms a cone on the ground such that the height of the cone is always one-third of the radius of the base. How fast is the height of the sand cone increasing at the instant when the height is 4 cm ?
rows.solution: Let the sand cone have height \(h\), base radius \(r\) and volume \(\mathrm{V}\) at time \(t\). Sand arrives at \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{V}}{dt} = 15\) cm\(^{3}\)/minute, and the shape condition "the height is always one-third of the radius" means \(h = \dfrac{r}{3}\), i.e. \(r = 3h\). Using this to eliminate \(r\), \(\mathrm{V} = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi (3h)^{2}h = 3\pi h^{3}\), which depends on \(h\) alone. Differentiating with respect to \(t\), \(\dfrac{d\mathrm{V}}{dt} = 9\pi h^{2}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\), so \(9\pi h^{2}\dfrac{dh}{dt} = 15\) and \(\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{5}{3\pi h^{2}}\). At the instant when \(h = 4\) cm, \(\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{5}{3\pi \times 16} = \dfrac{5}{48\pi}\) cm/minute, roughly \(0.033\) cm/minute.

rows.stem:
Find the values of a and b so that the following function is differentiable for all values of \(x\) :

\(\mathrm{f}(x) = \begin{cases} \mathrm{a}x + \mathrm{b}, & x > -1 \\ \mathrm{b}x^2 - 3, & x \le -1 \end{cases}\)
rows.solution: Each piece is a polynomial, so f is automatically differentiable everywhere except possibly at the join \(x = -1\); and since differentiability implies continuity, BOTH conditions have to hold there. Continuity at \(x = -1\): the left-hand limit, which is also the value, is \(\lim_{x \to -1^{-}}\left(\mathrm{b}x^{2} - 3\right) = \mathrm{b} - 3 = \mathrm{f}(-1)\), while the right-hand limit is \(\lim_{x \to -1^{+}}\left(\mathrm{a}x + \mathrm{b}\right) = -\mathrm{a} + \mathrm{b}\). Equating them, \(\mathrm{b} - 3 = -\mathrm{a} + \mathrm{b}\), so \(\mathrm{a} = 3\). Differentiability at \(x = -1\): the left-hand derivative is \(\lim_{x \to -1^{-}}\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{b}x^{2} - 3\right) - \left(\mathrm{b} - 3\right)}{x + 1} = \lim_{x \to -1^{-}}\dfrac{\mathrm{b}\left(x^{2} - 1\right)}{x + 1} = \lim_{x \to -1^{-}}\mathrm{b}(x - 1) = -2\mathrm{b}\), and the right-hand derivative, using \(\mathrm{a} = 3\), is \(\lim_{x \to -1^{+}}\dfrac{\left(\mathrm{a}x + \mathrm{b}\right) - \left(\mathrm{b} - 3\right)}{x + 1} = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}}\dfrac{3x + 3}{x + 1} = 3\). Equating the two gives \(-2\mathrm{b} = 3\), so \(\mathrm{b} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\). Check: with \(\mathrm{a} = 3\) and \(\mathrm{b} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\) both branches give \(\mathrm{f}(-1) = -\dfrac{9}{2}\), and the two one-sided derivatives are \(-3x\big|_{x=-1} = 3\) and \(3\), which agree. [CBSE marking scheme: its main route and its answers \(\mathrm{a} = 3\), \(\mathrm{b} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\) are correct, but in the "Alternately" route the RHD is printed with the SAME difference quotient as the LHD, namely \(\dfrac{\mathrm{f}(-1) - \mathrm{f}(-1-h)}{h}\), whereas the algebra written underneath it is \(\dfrac{\mathrm{f}(-1+h) - \mathrm{f}(-1)}{h}\). The two one-sided derivatives cannot come from one and the same quotient, so that label is a printing slip.]

rows.stem: Given \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{c} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\). Find a vector \(\vec{d}\) which is perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) and \(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d} = 3\).
rows.solution: A vector perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) must be parallel to their cross product, so write \(\vec{d} = \lambda\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right)\). With \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}\left[(-1)(-1) - (1)(0)\right] - \hat{j}\left[(2)(-1) - (1)(3)\right] + \hat{k}\left[(2)(0) - (-1)(3)\right] = \hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\). So \(\vec{d} = \lambda\left(\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\right)\), and the second condition fixes \(\lambda\): \(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d} = \lambda\left[(2)(1) + (1)(5) + (-2)(3)\right] = \lambda(2 + 5 - 6) = \lambda\), and this must equal 3, so \(\lambda = 3\). Hence \(\vec{d} = 3\hat{i} + 15\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}\). Checking all three requirements: \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{d} = 6 - 15 + 9 = 0\), \(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{d} = 9 + 0 - 9 = 0\) and \(\vec{c} \cdot \vec{d} = 6 + 15 - 18 = 3\).

rows.stem: Bag I contains 3 red and 4 black balls, Bag II contains 5 red and 2 black balls. Two balls are transferred at random from Bag I to Bag II and then a ball is drawn at random from Bag II. Find the probability that the drawn ball is red in colour.
rows.solution: Condition on what gets transferred, since that is what changes Bag II. Bag I holds 3 red and 4 black, so the two balls moved across fall into three cases: \(\mathrm{E}_{1}\), both red; \(\mathrm{E}_{2}\), both black; \(\mathrm{E}_{3}\), one red and one black. There are \({}^{7}C_{2} = 21\) equally likely pairs, so \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{{}^{3}C_{2}}{21} = \dfrac{3}{21} = \dfrac{1}{7}\), \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{{}^{4}C_{2}}{21} = \dfrac{6}{21} = \dfrac{2}{7}\) and \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{E}_{3}\right) = \dfrac{3 \times 4}{21} = \dfrac{4}{7}\); these sum to 1, as they must. Let A be the event that the ball finally drawn from Bag II is red. Bag II starts with 5 red and 2 black and always contains \(7 + 2 = 9\) balls after the transfer, so \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}\mid\mathrm{E}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{7}{9}\) (5 red plus the 2 transferred), \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}\mid\mathrm{E}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{9}\) and \(\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A}\mid\mathrm{E}_{3}\right) = \dfrac{6}{9}\). By the theorem of total probability, \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) = \dfrac{1}{7}\times\dfrac{7}{9} + \dfrac{2}{7}\times\dfrac{5}{9} + \dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{7 + 10 + 24}{63} = \dfrac{41}{63}\).

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following Linear Programming problem graphically :

Maximise \(\mathrm{Z} = 300x + 600\mathrm{y}\)

Subject to \(x + 2\mathrm{y} \le 12\)

\(2x + \mathrm{y} \le 12\)

\(x + \dfrac{5}{4}\mathrm{y} \ge 5\)

\(x \ge 0,\ \mathrm{y} \ge 0\).
rows.solution: Draw the three boundary lines \(x + 2\mathrm{y} = 12\), \(2x + \mathrm{y} = 12\) and \(x + \dfrac{5}{4}\mathrm{y} = 5\) (equivalently \(4x + 5\mathrm{y} = 20\)) in the first quadrant. The origin satisfies the first two inequalities, so the feasible region lies on or below those two lines; it fails \(x + \dfrac{5}{4}\mathrm{y} \ge 5\), so the region lies on the far side of the third line from the origin. Together with \(x \ge 0\) and \(\mathrm{y} \ge 0\) this is a bounded pentagon, so the maximum is attained at a corner point. On the Y-axis, \(x + \dfrac{5}{4}\mathrm{y} = 5\) gives \(\mathrm{A}(0, 4)\) and \(x + 2\mathrm{y} = 12\) gives \(\mathrm{B}(0, 6)\); on the X-axis, \(2x + \mathrm{y} = 12\) gives \(\mathrm{D}(6, 0)\) and \(x + \dfrac{5}{4}\mathrm{y} = 5\) gives \(\mathrm{E}(5, 0)\); and solving \(x + 2\mathrm{y} = 12\) together with \(2x + \mathrm{y} = 12\) gives the fifth corner \(\mathrm{C}(4, 4)\). Evaluating \(\mathrm{Z} = 300x + 600\mathrm{y}\) at each: \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{A}) = 2400\), \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{B}) = 3600\), \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{C}) = 1200 + 2400 = 3600\), \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{D}) = 1800\) and \(\mathrm{Z}(\mathrm{E}) = 1500\). The greatest value is 3600 and it occurs at TWO corners, B and C. Whenever that happens the optimum is attained along the whole edge joining them: the segment BC lies on \(x + 2\mathrm{y} = 12\), and there \(\mathrm{Z} = 300\left(x + 2\mathrm{y}\right) = 300 \times 12 = 3600\) identically. Hence the maximum value of Z is 3600, attained at every point of the line segment BC joining \((0, 6)\) and \((4, 4)\).
